A bauble is a small, shiny, decorative object that looks attractive but has little or no real value. Think of something that catches your eye, maybe even makes you say "oh, pretty!" — but when you pick it up and think about it, it's essentially worthless. Cheap, trivial, but eye-catching. That is the soul of a bauble.

1. A cheap, showy trinket or ornament

This is the broadest and most fundamental meaning. A bauble is a small decorative item — like a glittery brooch, a sparkly charm, a gaudy little figurine, or any bit of cheap jewelry — that has more flash than substance. The key combination is: looks fancy, isn't worth much.

Imagine a market stall covered in shiny little objects: plastic gems, fake-gold pendants, tiny colourful objects. Those are baubles. They dazzle at first glance but have no real worth.

2. A Christmas tree ornament (especially in British English)

In everyday modern British usage, a bauble most commonly refers to those round, shiny balls you hang on a Christmas tree — the hollow spheres made of glass or plastic, often in red, gold, silver, or other bright colours, that reflect light and make the tree look festive. If a British person says "we hung baubles on the tree," they mean these decorations.

This usage fits perfectly with the word's core meaning: Christmas baubles are visually appealing and festive, but each one individually is a trivial, inexpensive little thing.

3. A jester's mock scepter (historical)

In older, historical usage, a bauble referred to the short stick or mock-scepter carried by a court jester (the professional fool who entertained royalty in medieval times). This stick was typically decorated with a carved head, ribbons, or bells, and it was a prop of foolishness and comedy. It was called a bauble because — just like a shiny trinket — it looked like a symbol of power (a real king carries a scepter), but it was actually a silly, meaningless object meant to mock the very idea of importance.

You're most likely to encounter this meaning when reading older literature, Shakespeare, or historical texts. It's not a common everyday usage today.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

Here's something important: bauble carries a slightly dismissive or condescending tone. When someone calls something a bauble, they're not just saying it's decorative — they're subtly suggesting it's frivolous, trivial, or not worth taking seriously.

The word implies a kind of surface-level sparkle that hides a lack of real depth or importance. It's the verbal equivalent of rolling your eyes at something flashy.

Because of this dismissive tone, bauble is also used figuratively to describe anything — not just a physical object — that seems impressive or valuable but is actually trivial or meaningless.

For example:

  • A critic might call a prestigious-but-empty award "a mere bauble" — meaning it looks impressive but doesn't really signify anything worthwhile.
  • Someone could dismissively say a politician's achievement is "just a bauble" — meaning it's a shiny, feel-good thing with no real substance.

In this figurative sense, you could apply the word to titles, honours, achievements, possessions, or anything else you want to suggest is more flashy than meaningful.

• "She came home from the fair with a bag full of cheap baubles she'd never use." — trinkets with no real value.
  • "The children spent the afternoon hanging red and gold baubles on the Christmas tree." — tree ornaments.
  • "The king dismissed the jester, who juggled his bauble and somersaulted out of the hall." — the jester's mock-scepter.
  • "He called the trophy a bauble — a hollow reward for a meaningless competition." — figurative use, suggesting something is trivial despite appearing impressive.

If you can only hold on to one idea, hold on to this: a bauble is something small, shiny, and decorative that looks more valuable or important than it actually is. Whether it's a cheap ornament, a Christmas ball, or anything else you want to call trivial — the word always carries that same undercurrent: pretty, but not worth much.
